611.quote_or_event: “So tell me - how can the fort of doubt and the moat of Maya be overcome? … Worshipping the Perfect Guru, this awesome force is subdued.”
611.explanation: In a pauri of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan describes the five passions as an army no hero can withstand, asks how such a fortress could ever be breached, and answers that it can be overcome.
611.tie_back: The Kural says never lose heart because a task looks too hard; Guru Arjan names the hardest of tasks and refuses to call it impossible.
611.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, pauri 15), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
611._accuracy_note: Shares the refusal to call a hard task impossible, but in Gurbani the victory comes through devotion to the Guru rather than through the person's own exertion, which is the Kural's point.

612.quote_or_event: “Let self-control be the furnace, and patience the goldsmith.”
612.explanation: In the closing pauri of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak pictures the shaping of a true life as a goldsmith's long work at the furnace, carried out with patience and steady control.
612.tie_back: The Kural warns against letting effort slacken halfway through a task; Japji Sahib makes patience the craftsman who keeps working until the piece is finished.
612.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Japji Sahib (pauri 38), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
612._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the verse values patient, sustained work, but it describes the forging of spiritual character, not finishing a worldly undertaking, and says nothing of the world abandoning those who give up.

613.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
613.explanation: In a salok in Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak links giving to honest labour: the person who earns his bread by his own work and shares part of it is the one who has found the right way.
613.tie_back: The Kural rests the power to help others on hard work alone; Guru Nanak likewise makes earned livelihood (kirat karni) the ground of sharing (vand chhakna).
613.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang (Saarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
613._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both texts make one's own labour the foundation of generosity; Gurbani adds that this is the spiritual path, not only a social distinction.

614.quote_or_event: “The thief robs a house, and offers the stolen goods to his ancestors. In the world hereafter, this is recognized, and his ancestors are considered thieves as well.”
614.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak mocks charity given out of wealth one did not honestly earn: the gift is recognised for what it is and brings shame instead of merit.
614.tie_back: The Kural says generosity without one's own effort fails like a sword in timid hands; Guru Nanak says giving that does not come from one's own honest earning is worthless.
614.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
614._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Guru Nanak's target is stolen wealth and ritual offerings to ancestors, while the Kural's is the idle would-be benefactor; both make honest effort the condition of real giving.

615.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
615.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan praises seva done for its own sake, with no thought of reward for oneself.
615.tie_back: The Kural praises the one who craves the work rather than his own pleasure and so holds up his kin; Guru Arjan praises service done with no thought of reward for oneself.
615.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauree (Sukhmani Sahib), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
615._accuracy_note: Next-best: the shared idea is self-forgetting work, but the verse concerns service of the Guru and union with God, not supporting one's family, which is the Kural's image of the pillar.

616.quote_or_event: “Make the effort, and you shall live; practicing it, you shall enjoy peace. Meditating, you shall meet God, O Nanak, and your anxiety shall vanish.”
616.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar, Guru Arjan uses the word udam (effort, exertion) and promises that the one who makes the effort and keeps practising it will gain life and peace.
616.tie_back: The Kural says effort brings prosperity and idleness brings want; Guru Arjan likewise says effort brings life and peace and puts anxiety to flight.
616.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 522, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
616._accuracy_note: Strong fit on effort as the source of wellbeing; the effort Guru Arjan means is chiefly meditation on the Name, and the reward is spiritual peace rather than material wealth.

617.quote_or_event: “Cheated and plundered by Maya, you do not think of God, and you waste your life in laziness.”
617.explanation: In a hymn of Bhagat Trilochan included in the Guru Granth Sahib, the idle person is pictured as robbed and ruined, his life squandered through laziness.
617.tie_back: The Kural says misfortune dwells in sloth; Trilochan's hymn likewise shows laziness leaving a person plundered and his life wasted.
617.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 92, Siree Raag, Bhagat Trilochan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
617._accuracy_note: Next-best: the link between sloth and loss matches, but the Kural's image of goddesses of misfortune and fortune has no place in Sikh teaching, and the loss Trilochan means is spiritual.

618.quote_or_event: “Dadda: Do not blame anyone else; blame instead your own actions.”
618.explanation: In his acrostic Patti, Guru Nanak teaches that a person should not lay blame on others but look at the record of his own deeds.
618.tie_back: The Kural says there is no disgrace in bad luck, only in failing to make the effort; Guru Nanak likewise places responsibility on one's own actions, not on outside causes.
618.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 433, Raag Aasaa (Patti), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
618._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both shift the question from fortune to one's own conduct, but Guru Nanak is concerned with blaming others rather than with luck, and Gurbani elsewhere gives a large place to hukam and grace.

619.quote_or_event: “They receive the wages of their labor, begging at the Door of their Lord and Master.”
619.explanation: In a salok of Soohee ki Vaar, Guru Nanak speaks of devotees who labour and receive the wages of that labour at the Lord's door.
619.tie_back: The Kural says that even when fate blocks the goal, effort still pays the wages of the body's toil; Guru Nanak likewise speaks of labour that is paid its wage.
619.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Raag Soohee (Soohee ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
619._accuracy_note: Next-best: the image of labour earning its wage matches, but the verse says nothing about effort paying off even against fate, and the wage is received as the Lord's gift rather than as a right won by effort.

620.quote_or_event: “He alone is known as a spiritual hero, who fights in defense of religion. He may be cut apart, piece by piece, but he never leaves the field of battle.”
620.explanation: In a hymn of Bhagat Kabir in Raag Maaroo, often recited by Sikhs, the true hero is the one who never gives up the fight, whatever it costs him.
620.tie_back: The Kural promises that those who strive without faltering will see even fate turn its back; Kabir praises the one who never leaves the field, even when cut to pieces.
620.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
620._accuracy_note: Next-best: it matches the unflagging persistence, but says nothing about defeating fate; in Sikh teaching the inscribed destiny gives way to God's grace and hukam, not to human effort alone, so the Kural's boldest claim has no exact Sikh parallel.
